To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a genetic profile consisting of three SNPs can be used to predict which patients with head-and-neck cancer are most likely to benefit from 13-cis retinoic acid (RA) therapy; (ii) this genetic profile can also be used to identify which patients with head and neck cancer are most likely not to benefit from this therapy; and (iii) the genetic profile may be useful for predicting which head-and-neck patients are most likely to develop second primary tumors or cancer recurrence.

(i) a new, personalized, risk-based approach to cancer prevention has been demonstrated in a phase III clinical trial, (ii) the approach is based on genetic information and is not limited to the use of any particular drug, (iii) the approach is effective in the prevention of second primary tumors and the recurrence of cancer, (iv) the approach is applicable to other cancers and other drugs, and (v) the approach is cost-effective.
the 13-cis retinoic acid (isotretinoin) treatment effect in the head and neck trial was highly dependent upon the genetic profile of an individual.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of genetic and epigenetic factors that influence the risk of second primary tumors (STPs) and/or treatment-related toxicity in patients who have completed treatment for head-and-neck cancer (HNC).
identifying the genetic and molecular basis of individual variation in the risk and outcome of cancer.
the development of a new approach to the development of a cancer prevention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study by Lee et al. provides evidence that the genetic profile of a patient with HNSCC may predict the benefit of chemoprevention with 13-cRA and that this benefit is independent of smoking status.

the study reported by Lee et al. provides a strong case that a personalized approach to cancer prevention is feasible, but that further research is required to validate the results and to determine whether a similar approach could be applied to other cancers.

this is an important and novel study that has identified a number of SNPs that are associated with risk of second primary tumors and recurrence in patients who have been previously treated for squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the study by Lee et al. (1) is a landmark in cancer prevention.

we have shown for the first time that a targeted approach to prevention of a second primary tumor (SPT) in head and neck cancer (HNC) patients is feasible and that it is associated with a significant reduction in the risk of SPTs in patients who are genetically predisposed.
we have identified genetic variants that are associated with the risk of second primary tumors in the placebo group and with response to 13-cRA in the treatment arm of the study.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have identified a set of SNPs that are associated with risk of second primary tumors (or recurrence of primary head-and-neck cancer) and with response to the chemopreventive agent 13-cis retinoic acid.
we need to develop a new generation of cancer prevention strategies that can be tailored to individuals based on their genetic profiles.
